item.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervenes
item.description:
Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO effective immediately, less than two weeks after he resigned on November 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs. The board said it was satisfied with Huang's candor and ability to lead after a series of meetings, and noted it had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government and was confident his return poses no national security risk.

The reversal followed direct intervention from President Trump, who called into a board meeting hours before the vote to argue for Huang's return and later said Huang "did nothing wrong." Nvidia's stock jumped more than 30% on the news, and employees greeted Huang's return to headquarters with chants as he apologized for "putting all of you through all of this." The episode caps a remarkable about-face: the board had previously said it had no intention of reinstating him.

item.title: Ted Lasso officially renewed for season 5
item.description:
Apple has officially confirmed that Ted Lasso will return for a fifth season on Apple TV. The renewal had been widely expected — season four drew nearly 300 million U.S. viewing minutes across two days — but Apple had not formally announced it until now.

Production is reportedly aiming to begin in April, though no release date has been set. Jason Sudeikis returns as the title character, with the fourth season having brought Lasso back to England to coach a women's team, the AFC Richmond Lady Greyhounds. The show remains one of Apple TV's most popular series ever.

item.title: (PRODUCT)RED returns with red HomePod mini 2 and AirPods Max 2
item.description:
Apple is bringing back (PRODUCT)RED with special editions of the HomePod mini 2 and AirPods Max 2, according to Bloomberg. The launch is expected on or around December 1, World AIDS Day, as part of the charity's 20th anniversary year.

The red HomePod mini 2 will reportedly have a red mesh exterior, while the AirPods Max 2 edition pairs a silver finish with white ear cushions and headband and a red Digital Crown. Apple has supported the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria for 20 years, with a portion of (PRODUCT)RED sales funding its programs. It is the first (PRODUCT)RED hardware in some time, and the first time the branding has appeared on a HomePod or AirPods Max.

item.title: 55,000 EU businesses urge crackdown on Apple's iPhone browser rules
item.description:
A coalition led by Mozilla and Shopify, representing up to 55,000 European businesses and organizations, is urging the European Commission to open formal enforcement proceedings against Apple over iPhone browser competition.

In an open letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the group argues that Apple's changes under the Digital Markets Act have failed to deliver real browser choice. More than two and a half years after the DMA took effect, no browser vendor has managed to move its existing EU users off Apple's WebKit engine to its own engine, the coalition says, because Apple's rules still make switching effectively impractical. The letter also claims Apple's restrictions hamper selling subscriptions outside the App Store. The Commission has not yet said whether it will act.

Sources

  • AppleInsider News: EU urged to challenge Apple's grip on iPhone browsers

item.title: iOS 27.2 and 27.3 add Photos, Apple Pay, and app updates
item.description:
Apple's recent and upcoming iPhone software updates add a batch of everyday improvements. iOS 27.2, already out, upgrades Apple Photos in two ways, while the forthcoming iOS 27.3 adds new features across six built-in apps. Apple Pay is also getting four new features, plus a major expansion rolling out now.

Smaller quality-of-life changes stand out too: iOS 27 adds an independent volume setting for alarms, so a quiet media volume can no longer leave you sleeping through your wake-up call. And GymKit is expanding beyond the Apple Watch — with iOS 27, an iPhone paired with AirPods Pro 3 can exchange heart rate and workout metrics with compatible gym equipment, much like the watch-based experience.

item.title: Berkshire Hathaway keeps Apple as its biggest stock bet
item.description:
Berkshire Hathaway has stopped selling Apple shares, leaving the iPhone maker as its largest stock investment a decade after it first bought in. After selling down its stake through 2024 and 2025, Berkshire held its Apple position unchanged through September 2026 under its new CEO.

Apple's stock is up 29% this year and now accounts for roughly a quarter of Berkshire's public stock portfolio. Warren Buffett first bought Apple in 2016, and the holding has long been Berkshire's biggest single bet — a vote of confidence that stands out as Berkshire has been actively trading the rest of its largest positions.

item.title: Apple's spring 2027 lineup looks huge: iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, MacBook Neo 2, and more

Apple's spring 2027 launch season is shaping up to be unusually busy. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the company plans to unveil the iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, an updated entry-level iPad, and new MacBook Neo and MacBook Air models around February or March, alongside the 27.4 system software cycle. A second wave — iPhone Air 2 and new iPad Air and iPad Pro models — would follow a little later, possibly in March or April.

The MacBook Neo 2, codenamed J701, is expected around March with possible new colors, and Apple reportedly plans to update it annually. After a busy fall, Apple apparently has no intention of slowing down: spring 2027 could bring more new hardware than the fall did.

item.title: Siri layoffs spared the newer AI teams — but Siri's problems persist
item.description:
Apple's recent Siri layoffs hit employees working on the assistant's older infrastructure rather than its newer AI systems, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman — but employees have yet to notice a major difference in how Apple operates, despite efforts to accelerate development and spread big releases throughout the year. Gurman adds that Apple faces growing competition from AI developers who update their models and services far more frequently than Apple's annual OS cycle.

Meanwhile, AppleInsider's Sunday Reboot notes Apple's pettiness is on full display in the UK, where Apple decided not to extend Siri AI limit increases to the country — for reasons that remain unclear. The two stories together paint the familiar picture: Siri's rebuild is real, but the pace and the polish still lag the competition.

item.title: iOS 27 has a clever fix for unreliable Wi-Fi
item.description:
iOS 27 includes a clever new feature aimed at the awkward middle ground between cellular and Wi-Fi: those moments when your phone clings to a weak, barely-working Wi-Fi network instead of switching to cellular. The feature addresses the unreliable-connection problem that has frustrated iPhone users for years — the phone that shows full Wi-Fi bars while nothing loads.

It's a small quality-of-life fix rather than a headline feature, but it's the kind of thing that quietly makes a phone feel better every day. 9to5Mac has the details on how it works and how to turn it on.

Sources

item.title: iPhone Duo could get a 'complication column' of Lock Screen widgets, leak suggests
item.description:
Apple has tested an experimental iPhone Duo Lock Screen layout that would let widgets occupy two separate areas, according to the leaker known as "pdfu." The unreleased layout, called a "Complication Column," adds a vertical pair of circular widgets along the right edge of the screen — and crucially, it can be used together with the existing bottom widget row, giving users access to more information at a glance.

Apple already reworked iOS for the Duo's form factor, including a revamped Lock Screen. Whether the complication column ships is still unknown — Apple tests plenty of ideas that never reach customers — but it's a sign the company is still exploring how much glanceable information the Duo's larger canvas can hold.

item.title: Google's AI search problem is costing Apple revenue
item.description:
Apple's Safari search deal with Google isn't as lucrative as it once was — and the cause isn't a falling-out between the two companies. Users are changing how they search, increasingly relying on AI answers instead of traditional search results, and Google's AI search isn't monetizing the way classic search did.

That matters because the deal, worth around $20 billion a year for Google to be Safari's default search engine, has been one of Apple's most profitable arrangements — and one that already drew a DOJ antitrust lawsuit. If AI changes search behavior faster than Google can monetize it, Apple's cut shrinks too. The shift in how people find information is quietly becoming a revenue problem for both companies.

Sources

item.title: Siri AI settlement: expect at least $61 per iPhone
item.description:
Apple agreed in May to pay $250 million to settle a U.S. class action over Siri AI's delayed launch, and there's now one month left to file a claim through the settlement website. Court documents filed this week say claimants will likely receive at least $61 per eligible iPhone, based on early participation data, with the exact amount depending on how many valid claims come in — up to a maximum of $95 per device.

The payout is a modest consolation for owners who bought iPhones expecting the AI-powered Siri Apple promoted, only to see its launch slip badly. If you haven't filed yet, the window closes in about a month, so it's worth checking your eligibility now rather than waiting for the deadline to creep up.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Siri AI Settlement: Here's How Much Apple Will Pay You

item.title: Apple Intelligence gets paywalled tiers: iCloud+ buys more AI
item.description:
Apple has published a support document spelling out what was previously only implied: starting with the 2027 software releases, Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are free on supported devices, but the server-powered features have usage limits — and higher limits come with paid iCloud+ plans, beginning with the 27.3 release. Affected features include Siri AI image tools like Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing, Image Playground, and the cloud models in Shortcuts workflows and automation.

This is the clearest sign yet that Apple is moving toward a freemium model for its most powerful AI features, with iCloud+ as the subscription lever. It's a notable shift from Apple's usual pitch of on-device, private AI, and it means heavy users of the cloud-backed tools will eventually hit a paywall — or a subscription prompt.

Sources

item.title: iOS and macOS 27.3 betas: Face Unlock for iPhone Duo, tougher privacy controls
item.description:
Apple's second betas of the 27.3 releases bring two noteworthy changes. On the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 adds a facial unlock option — addressing one of the biggest complaints about the foldable, which launched without Apple's usual face-based authentication. On the Mac, macOS 27.3 tightens privacy controls around Full Disk Access and apps that control other apps, with a week of hands-on use finding them good overall, save for the ever-present menu bar indicator that flags apps controlling other apps.

Neither change is flashy, but both fix real annoyances: Duo owners finally get the unlock experience iPhone users expect, and Mac users get clearer guardrails over which apps can reach deep into their system. Expect the 27.3 releases to ship in the coming weeks as Apple wraps up its software year.

item.title: Looking to 2027: iPhone Air 2 gains a second camera
item.description:
If you're skipping this year's iPhone 18 Pro or the hard-to-get iPhone Duo, next year's lineup may be worth the wait. The most concrete detail to emerge so far: dummy models of the iPhone Air 2 show a second rear camera, addressing the single-camera compromise that was the original Air's biggest trade-off.

A second camera would make the Air a far more complete phone rather than a thinness-first novelty, and it suggests Apple heard the criticism that the first Air asked buyers to give up too much. Broader 2027 plans point to updates across most of Apple's existing products, but the Air 2's camera upgrade is the clearest reason yet to hold off if you were on the fence about this year's models.

item.title: Apple Support Community is gone for good
item.description:
Apple's Support Community forums are officially dead. After being placed in read-only mode on November 10, discussions.apple.com has now been removed entirely and redirects visitors to the main Apple Support page. The French and German forums are still accepting posts for now, but the English-language community — a fixture for troubleshooting help for years — is gone.

The closure ends a long-running, user-powered support resource that many people turned to before calling Apple or booking a Genius Bar visit. With it gone, users will lean more heavily on Apple's own support articles and chat, or on third-party forums like MacRumors and Reddit, for the kind of peer troubleshooting the community provided.

item.title: iPhone Air 2 dummy units show a dual-camera redesign
item.description:
Dummy models of the iPhone Air 2 and iPhone 18 have surfaced ahead of their expected spring 2027 launch, giving an early look at Apple's next round of phones. The big change is on the Air 2: it moves from a single rear camera to two lenses arranged horizontally on its raised camera plateau, addressing the original iPhone Air's most-criticized weakness. The standard iPhone 18, meanwhile, looks largely unchanged from the iPhone 17.

The dummies, shared by leaker Sonny Dickson, fit Apple's shift to a twice-yearly iPhone cadence: the Pro models and the iPhone Duo launched in September 2026, with the Air 2 and standard iPhone 18 following in early 2027. Dummy units are early and not always final, but three outlets reaching the same conclusion makes the dual-camera Air a fairly safe bet.

item.title: Apple can finally admit the UK forced it to weaken iCloud encryption
item.description:
Apple can at last confirm what was widely suspected: when it restricted iCloud Advanced Data Protection for new users in the UK in February 2025, it did so because the British government demanded a backdoor into encrypted iCloud data. A gag order had prevented Apple from saying so until now.

The admission closes a strange chapter in which Apple disabled its strongest encryption option for UK users while being legally barred from explaining why. It also puts the UK's Investigatory Powers Act back in the spotlight, since the demand reportedly sought access not just to UK users' data but to encrypted data globally. Apple has long argued that building such access for one government means building it for all of them.

Sources

  • Six Colors: Finally, Apple can reveal the UK backdoor demand

item.title: Siri Recap is private, but not very useful yet
item.description:
Apple's new Siri Recap feature, now in testing in the watchOS 27.3 beta on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, listens to nearby conversations and generates a brief summary of what was discussed. The privacy design is genuinely strict: audio is sectioned off from apps, Apple, and the rest of the OS, then discarded once a summary is generated.

After two weeks of testing, though, MacRumors found the privacy safeguards sharply limit the feature's usefulness. Summaries are overly brief, speakers aren't labeled, and there's no original audio to check against, making the recaps unreliable for anything that matters. It's a promising idea that currently reads more like a privacy proof-of-concept than a tool you'd trust to remember a meeting for you.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Siri Recap Hands-On: Private, But Not Very Useful

item.title: iOS 27 lets two iPhones share one phone number
item.description:
Among iOS 27's many additions is a quiet but genuinely useful one for people with two iPhones: iPhone Handoff now lets you keep the same phone number active on both devices. Previously, a second iPhone meant a second number or a juggling act with SIMs and eSIMs; now both phones can receive calls and messages on the same line.

The feature arrives alongside iOS 27.3, currently in beta, which also brings a redesigned Health app and new iPhone Duo features — including an optional front-camera unlock for the closed foldable, added in beta 2. It's a reminder that the most welcome iOS changes are often the small, practical ones rather than the headline features.

item.title: Microsoft is killing To Do, and there's no good Mac alternative
item.description:
Microsoft will retire its To Do apps on June 30, 2027, ending support on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, Android, and the web. Work and school account users are being directed to Microsoft Planner inside Teams — but personal Microsoft accounts, including Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers, can't access Planner at all, leaving them to find a new task manager entirely.

Worse, switching to Planner won't migrate existing tasks and lists; they'll remain visible in Planner only until the June 2027 cutoff, then vanish. It's the end of the line for an app that began as Wunderlist, which Microsoft bought in 2015 and rebranded in 2017. If you rely on To Do, now is the time to export your lists and pick a replacement.

  • MacRumors: Microsoft to Retire 'To Do' Apps Next Year

item.title: TSMC suspends advanced chip orders for Chinese firms under tighter US rules
item.description:
TSMC, which manufactures Apple's A- and M-series chips, has suspended some advanced chip orders for Chinese companies after the US tightened semiconductor export restrictions. Under the revised rules, TSMC can no longer supply Chinese firms with chips built on 16nm processes or smaller unless a US export license is granted or an exemption applies.

The move further squeezes China's access to cutting-edge silicon and puts TSMC — caught between its biggest customer base in the West and a major market in China — in an awkward middle. For Apple, the direct impact is limited, since its own chips aren't affected; the significance is geopolitical, as the chip supply chain continues to split along US-China lines.

Sources

  • AppleInsider: Apple supplier TSMC cuts off China chip orders amid tighter export controls

item.title: Signal now blocks screenshots to keep Siri AI out of your chats
item.description:
Signal has rolled out an update that automatically disables screenshots in the app, explicitly to stop Siri AI from reading private chats. Apple's on-device AI can access what's on screen, and Signal calls that an existential threat to the privacy its users expect.

The protection isn't complete — Signal admits gaps remain, including on macOS — but it's a striking escalation in the tension between AI assistants that see everything on your device and apps built around the promise that nobody else sees your messages. Expect other privacy-focused apps to follow, and expect Apple, Google, and Microsoft to face more pressure to give users a way to keep AI out of sensitive apps.

item.title: Apple is building an autonomous AI agent that can use apps and write code
item.description:
Apple is hiring engineers to build its own autonomous AI agent, according to job listings spotted by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The listing describes an agent that works the way a capable person would: browsing the web, working across apps, running commands, writing and debugging code, and calling services — choosing the right tool for each step.

It's the clear next step from the Siri and Apple Intelligence work already underway, which is wiring up app intents so Apple's software can act on your behalf. Apple is late to a market OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google have already entered. There's no public timeline — Apple is still staffing up, starting with a senior engineering leader — but the direction is unmistakable.

item.title: UK tribunal rules Apple can reveal the secret order demanding access to encrypted data
item.description:
The UK's Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled that Apple may publicly discuss a secret government order demanding access to its customers' encrypted data, rejecting the Home Office's attempt to keep the order hidden. The tribunal found the government failed to demonstrate that confirming the demand would damage national security, and the Home Office must now acknowledge that it served Apple with a technical capability notice — an order that can compel companies to make customer data accessible to security services.

The order itself was an open secret: Apple had already signaled it by withdrawing its Advanced Data Protection feature in the UK rather than comply. The ruling means Apple's legal challenge to the demand itself can now be heard largely in public, a significant win for transparency in a case the government fought hard to keep behind closed doors.

item.title: Jon McCormack, Apple's head of iPhone camera software, has retired
item.description:
Jon McCormack, Apple's vice president of camera and photo software engineering, retired at the end of October after more than eight years at the company, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports. McCormack joined Apple in 2018 from Amazon and Hewlett-Packard and oversaw the iPhone's Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how users capture, view, and edit their pictures and video.

He was a low-profile figure despite the importance of the role — a photographer and conservationist who was only occasionally interviewed publicly about his work. His departure leaves big shoes to fill at a moment when computational photography is central to the iPhone's appeal, and no successor has been named in the reporting so far.

item.title: Google's Gemini can now control apps on your Mac — with security caveats
item.description:
Google expanded the Gemini app for Mac with computer-use capabilities, letting the AI take over your desktop to complete multi-step tasks in the background: clicking, typing, navigating menus, and filling in forms across local apps, files, and websites. It works in an isolated window with a live preview so you can watch what it's doing, you choose which apps it may use, and it asks for approval before taking key actions.

The convenience comes with real risk, and AppleInsider argues the trade-off isn't worth it: an agent with control of your apps and files is a powerful attack surface if it can be tricked or misled. Still, the move shows how fast agentic AI is arriving on the Mac — while Apple's own agent, per today's job listings, is still being built.

item.title: Apple may delay or cancel the OLED iMac as panel costs bite
item.description:
Apple is discussing delaying or scrapping its planned OLED iMac with display partner Samsung, according to The Elec, citing high panel costs and weaker-than-expected demand for OLED devices. The tandem OLED display in the new PROLED MacBook Pro has drawn praise, but the iPad Pro's OLED debut in 2024 failed to spark the expected sales surge, and Apple is reportedly rethinking whether an OLED iMac — previously eyed for 2029 or 2030 — is worth it. The talks are currently said to focus on delay rather than outright cancellation.

Longer term, there may be a cheaper path: LG Display is developing a new OLED process called FLiPP that packs pixels tighter for brighter, longer-lasting, lower-power panels, potentially reaching the MacBook Air and iMac around 2030.

item.title: Apple Support Community forums close Friday after 28 years
item.description:
Apple's Support Community discussion forums will close permanently on Friday, November 20, ending a 28-year run of user-to-user tech support. The forums are already in a read-only state, with new posts no longer accepted, and Apple says existing posts will eventually be removed entirely — though it's not clear whether that happens immediately on Friday or later.

The forums existed in some form since the late 1990s and were for years the first stop for Mac and iPhone owners troubleshooting problems with help from fellow users. Their closure marks the end of an era, with Apple steering support seekers toward its official support channels and documentation instead.

item.title: Senators press Apple over teens' access to AI 'nudify' apps
item.description:
Three U.S. senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta demanding answers about AI-powered "nudify" apps that generate nonconsensual nude images — and warning of congressional action if the companies don't crack down. The letters focus on how easily teens can access these apps through the major app stores and platforms, and ask what the companies are doing to prevent it.

Apple has responded to the pressure, though the details of its reply are still emerging. The episode puts Apple squarely in the middle of a growing political fight over app-store accountability for AI-generated sexual imagery, and it raises the prospect of new legislation if the companies' own moderation doesn't satisfy lawmakers.

item.title: iOS 27.3 will cap Siri AI usage — iCloud+ raises the limit, but not everywhere
item.description:
Apple will introduce daily usage limits for Siri's AI features in iOS 27.3, and this week's beta shows what hitting the cap actually looks like. Free users get a base allowance, while iCloud+ subscribers get a bigger one: double the limit on the 200GB plan, scaling up to 20 times the base allowance on the 12TB plan. The beta also clarifies which kinds of requests count toward the limit.

There's a catch for some users: Apple's support documentation says subscribers in the UK and certain other countries won't get the extra allowance at all, with no reason given. The change effectively turns Siri's AI into a metered, tiered service — generous for heavy iCloud+ subscribers in supported countries, but a real constraint for everyone else.

item.title: iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 point to a March launch as display production nears
item.description:
Apple's first spring iPhone launch is taking shape: supply-chain reports from Korea's ETNews say mass production of OLED displays for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 begins in January, pointing to a March 2027 release. That fits the new staggered schedule Apple adopted this fall, when only the high-end Pro and Duo models debuted and the standard models were held back.

The iPhone Air 2 is reportedly keeping the same display as its predecessor so Apple can use existing OLED panel inventory, suggesting a modest spec refresh rather than a redesign. Taken together, the reports make a spring launch for the two base models look increasingly firm — a first for the iPhone line.

item.title: Leaks sketch the 20th anniversary iPhone: titanium is back, glass curves to the edge
item.description:
Fresh leaks are filling in the picture of next fall's 20th anniversary iPhone — expected to be called the iPhone 20 — and it sounds like a major redesign. Leaker Fixed Focus Digital says the iPhone 20 Pro will return to a titanium frame with a more rounded design, while another leak claims the curved glass edges will be just about a millimeter thick, practically invisible from the front.

Leaker Ice Universe adds that Apple is developing four models with two different designs for the anniversary lineup: two with flat glass and two with a radical all-glass appearance. All of this is still rumor, and a year out the details are sure to shift — but the consensus is that the 20th anniversary phone will be the biggest iPhone redesign in years.

item.title: Apple's iCloud outage traced to an internal update, not a cyberattack
item.description:
Apple suffered a widespread service outage on Tuesday, with iCloud sign-ins, iCloud Mail, the App Store, Apple Business, AppleCare on Device, and some school services all affected from around 11:45 a.m. ET. Users reported being unable to sign in to their Apple Accounts, sync Photos and Notes, or complete purchases in Apple retail stores. Apple's System Status page listed eight issues, three of them full outages.

Apple later told Bloomberg the problems were caused by an unspecified "internal update" and were not a cyberattack, and that most systems had been restored. It's a reminder of how much of the Apple ecosystem depends on a single sign-in: when Apple Accounts falter, everything from device setup to in-store checkout goes with them.

item.title: Memory shortage could keep prices high through 2030 as Apple locks in Samsung supply
item.description:
Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping component prices — and potentially device prices — elevated. Apple is reportedly one of 14 customers that have locked in priority orders, but those contracts do not protect against market-driven price increases, and Apple is said to be close to signing a similar long-term DRAM deal with Samsung.

Apple had ridden out the global chip shortage for some time on existing orders, but by February 2026 it was reportedly paying double its previous DRAM rate. For buyers, the upshot is that the era of falling memory prices — and the device discounts that came with it — looks over for the foreseeable future.

item.title: Apple accused of silencing iPhone Duo supplier over display cracks
item.description:
Apple allegedly pressured component supplier Fine M-Tec to withdraw a public statement distancing itself from the display-cracking issue affecting some iPhone Duo units, according to The Elec. The Korean supplier, which makes internal metal plates supporting the foldable screen, had posted a statement last month denying that defects in its components were responsible for the failures, shortly before Apple itself acknowledged the problem.

The number of cracked screens appears small, but the allegation matters less for the scale of the defect than for what it suggests about Apple's handling of it: a supplier publicly pushing back on blame is unusual in Apple's orbit. Meanwhile, Apple has begun selling iPhone Duo replacement parts through its Self Service Repair store, and shipping estimates for new orders have improved to December 17–28, in time for the holidays.

item.title: Siri AI gets daily usage limits in 2027, with iCloud+ perks — except in the UK
item.description:
Apple has begun detailing how Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features that rely on powerful server models will be capped by daily usage limits from the 2027 software releases. The features remain free for users with a supported device, but heavy users will hit a daily cap unless they have increased access — which Apple says will be included with most iCloud+ plans at no additional cost in most countries.

The notable exception is the UK, where Apple says the increased access will not be available with iCloud+ plans, leaving UK users with no clear workaround for now. The limits arrive with iOS 27.3 next month, which also brings a redesigned Apple Health app. The move mirrors rivals that meter server-based AI; the UK carve-out will likely draw questions about a paid tier there.

item.title: 178 major websites compromised in attack targeting iPhone users
item.description:
Hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, a third-party platform companies use to test and customize their websites, to inject malicious JavaScript into the sites of 178 organizations — including the BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, Zoom, and Salesforce. The code was designed to steal cryptocurrency and credit card data, with one vector aimed at iPhones and iPads on older iOS versions.

Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far only a few thousand dollars appear to have been stolen. But the scale is striking: ordinary visitors to hugely popular sites were exposed without clicking anything suspicious. It's a reminder that the weakest link is often a third-party script a trusted site loads — and that keeping iOS updated is the simplest defense.

item.title: iPhone set to gain share in 2027 as the smartphone market shrinks
item.description:
Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year to roughly 270 million units, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a Morgan Stanley research report published November 16. That stands out against a bleak industry backdrop: worldwide shipments are expected to fall 5% to 1.04 billion units in 2027, following an estimated 13.8% contraction in 2026, driven by economic pressures and surging memory prices.

The forecast is a substantial downgrade from Morgan Stanley's previous expectation of 3.6% industry growth, yet Apple is expected to grow through the downturn — a sign of how its premium positioning and installed base insulate it from the price pressures hitting Android makers hardest. If it holds, Apple emerges from the slump with its largest-ever share of a shrinking market.

item.title: Google Wallet comes to iPhone — but without tap to pay
item.description:
Google Wallet is now available on iPhone in the United States, giving users a way to organize payment cards, tickets, boarding passes, and receipts in one place, with package tracking synced from Gmail and other Google apps. Users can also scan loyalty and membership cards with the camera to import them.

The catch is at the checkout counter: Google Wallet cannot be used for tap-to-pay purchases in stores, so Apple Pay remains the only option for contactless payments on iPhone. The app does work for online checkout anywhere Google Pay is accepted. It's a useful organizer for people deep in Google's ecosystem, but as a wallet replacement it stops well short — a limitation that reflects Apple's continued control over NFC payments on its devices.

item.title: HomeView teardown finds a device that's nearly impossible to repair
item.description:
iFixit's teardown of Apple's new HomeView smart home hub found a device that takes a step backward in repairability compared to the HomePod. Strong adhesive holds the display in place and was difficult to remove, opening the device damaged internal components, and a mix of Phillips and Torx screws in different sizes means several tools are needed to get inside. Speakers take up most of the space behind the display.

The teardown also revealed the differences between the two models: the wall-mounted version gets smaller speakers than the speaker-base model. For a device meant to sit on a wall or counter for years, the poor repairability is a notable blemish on Apple's first smart home hub — even as regulators push Apple on repair access.
